issues.legal_issue: A witness’s relationship to the victim or interest in the prosecution does not, by itself, justify rejecting the witness’s testimony.
material_facts: Two principal eyewitnesses were members of the victims’ families, and one of them was seriously injured during the incident.
The eyewitness accounts were consistent with one another.
The High Court rejected the eyewitnesses’ evidence because it considered them interested witnesses, without properly assessing their testimony.
issues.conclusion: The eyewitnesses’ evidence could not be rejected merely because they were interested; the court could assess it cautiously and allow a reasonable discount if required. The consistent evidence, particularly that of the injured eyewitness, was reliable and sufficient to implicate the accused.
issues.legal_principle: An interested eyewitness’s testimony is not to be rejected solely because of the witness’s interest; the court may exercise caution and make a reasonable discount when assessing it. The circumstances of an injured eyewitness’s presence and the consistency of the accounts are relevant to evaluating reliability. The Court relied on no named earlier cases or specific statutory provisions for this principle.

rule.if: appeal_against_acquittal and (eyewitnesses_are_interested or eyewitness_is_related_to_victim) and eyewitness_accounts_are_consistent and injured_eyewitness_supports_account

predicates.appeal_against_acquittal: The prosecution appealed after an appellate court acquitted the accused.
predicates.eyewitnesses_are_interested: One or more eyewitnesses had an interest in the prosecution because of their connection to the victims.
predicates.eyewitness_is_related_to_victim: One or more eyewitnesses were members of the victims’ families.
predicates.eyewitness_accounts_are_consistent: The eyewitnesses gave accounts that were consistent with one another.
predicates.injured_eyewitness_supports_account: An eyewitness was injured in the incident and supported the account of the occurrence.

issues.definition: When an acquittal appeal concerns consistent eyewitness accounts, including support from a related or injured witness, the witnesses’ interest alone does not require rejection of their testimony.

issues.legal_issue: Faulty investigation or irregularities concerning the recording of a report do not, by themselves, justify acquittal when strong substantive evidence establishes the prosecution case.
material_facts: The High Court relied on alleged investigative defects and doubt about when and how the initial report was recorded in acquitting the accused.
The Supreme Court found that the eyewitness evidence strongly established the prosecution case and that the alleged defects did not displace it.
issues.conclusion: Even assuming the investigation was faulty, that fact alone did not justify acquitting the accused in the face of the strong evidence establishing their guilt.
issues.legal_principle: A defect in investigation, or an alleged irregularity in recording the initial report, is not by itself a basis to acquit where the substantive evidence establishes the prosecution case. The Court relied on no named earlier cases or specific statutory provisions for this principle.

predicates.appeal_against_acquittal: The prosecution appealed after an appellate court acquitted the accused.
predicates.investigation_was_faulty_or_report_recor: The investigation was alleged to be defective, or the timing or manner of recording the initial report was disputed.
predicates.strong_substantive_evidence_established_: The evidence, including eyewitness testimony, strongly established the prosecution case.

issues.definition: When a prosecution appeal follows an acquittal and strong substantive evidence establishes the case, investigative defects or a dispute about the initial report alone do not warrant acquittal.

issues.legal_issue: An acquittal based on a cursory assessment that ignores material, consistent eyewitness evidence cannot stand when that evidence establishes the prosecution case.
material_facts: The trial court convicted the accused after finding that the eyewitnesses were present, their evidence was consistent, and the prosecution case was established.
The High Court acquitted the accused without properly engaging with the substance of the eyewitness evidence, relying instead on alleged investigative defects and minor discrepancies.
The Supreme Court found the eyewitness evidence sufficient to prove the prosecution case.
issues.conclusion: The High Court’s acquittal was set aside, the trial court’s convictions were restored, and the prosecution appeals were allowed.
issues.legal_principle: An appellate court must assess the substance of the evidence; a cursory approach that ignores material eyewitness testimony and rests on peripheral defects cannot sustain an acquittal where the evidence establishes the case. The Court relied on no named earlier cases or specific statutory provisions for this conclusion; it restored the trial convictions for offences charged under Sections 302, 149, 148 and 147 of the Indian Penal Code, as applicable to the accused.

rule.if: appeal_against_acquittal and appellate_court_ignored_material_eyewitness_evidence and eyewitness_evidence_established_the_case and acquittal_rest_on_peripheral_defects

predicates.appeal_against_acquittal: The prosecution appealed after an appellate court acquitted the accused.
predicates.appellate_court_ignored_material_eyewitn: The appellate court did not properly assess material eyewitness testimony.
predicates.eyewitness_evidence_established_the_case: The eyewitness evidence established the prosecution case.
predicates.acquittal_rest_on_peripheral_defects: The acquittal rested on peripheral investigative defects or minor discrepancies rather than an assessment of the substantive evidence.

issues.definition: When an appellate acquittal ignores material eyewitness evidence that establishes the case and rests on peripheral defects, the acquittal is set aside and the trial conviction is restored.
